title: Control disease and pest in stored seed

lessons.title: Preparing for and recognising contamination
lessons.html:
Preparing for and recognising contamination

Seed in storage is alive. It can be damaged by insects, fungi, rodents and birds, and by heat and moisture that make these problems worse. Damaged seed loses germination and value. A seed store full of hybrid maize or vegetable seed can be worth millions of rand, so stored seed must be protected and problems found early.

Main threats

ThreatSigns
Storage insects (weevils, grain moths, beetles)Holes in seed, webbing, dust, live insects, warm spots in bags
Storage fungiMusty smell, caking, discoloured seed, visible mould
RodentsDroppings, chewed bags, spilled seed, runways along walls
BirdsDroppings, feathers, nests in roofs

Preparing

  • Know the store layout, lot numbers and how long each lot has been stored.
  • Have a monitoring plan: insect traps, rodent bait station map, temperature and humidity readings, and regular visual checks.
  • Make sure inspection tools are ready: torch, sieve, probe or sampling spear, magnifier, thermometer, sample bags and record sheets.
  • Check that approved control products and PPE are available and that only trained, authorised people may apply them.

Assessing the nature of contamination

  1. Inspect bags and bins, starting with older lots and areas where problems were found before.
  2. Take samples from top, middle and bottom of stacks or bins and sieve them to find insects.
  3. Identify the pest or disease. Take specimens to a senior person or laboratory if unsure.
  4. Measure seed moisture and temperature. Hot spots and high moisture point to insect or fungal activity.
  5. Decide how far the problem has spread: one bag, one stack or the whole store.
  6. Record findings with lot numbers and locations.

lessons.title: Combating contamination safely
lessons.html:
Combating contamination safely

The control method depends on the pest, how severe the problem is and what the seed is for. Always use integrated pest management: combine hygiene, good storage conditions and chemical control only where needed.

Non-chemical measures

  • Hygiene: remove spilled seed, dust and old residues, which feed insects. Clean cracks and corners.
  • Isolation: move infested lots away from clean lots.
  • Cool, dry storage: insects and fungi grow slowly when seed is dry and cool. Improve ventilation and fix roof leaks.
  • Rodent proofing: close gaps under doors, keep stacks off the floor on pallets and away from walls so you can inspect around them.

Chemical control

Only products registered under Act 36 of 1947 for that use may be applied, by trained people, following the label exactly. Options may include approved surface treatments of the store, seed treatment with a registered product, or fumigation by a registered fumigation operator for serious infestations.

  • Read the label before use: target pests, rates, PPE, re-entry and any restrictions on seed for planting.
  • Wear the PPE on the label.
  • Fumigation is high risk. It must be done only by qualified fumigators with gas monitoring, warning signs and clearance procedures.
  • Rodent baits must be in secured bait stations, recorded on a map and checked regularly.

Never

  • Never use a product not registered for stored seed.
  • Never increase the dose to work faster.
  • Never treat seed that may be eaten or fed to animals without checking the label.
  • Never let untrained workers apply chemicals or enter fumigated areas.

If a worker shows signs of poisoning, follow the label first aid, move them to fresh air without endangering yourself and get medical help immediately with the label.

lessons.title: Completing the control process
lessons.html:
Completing the control process

Control work is not finished when the product has been applied. You must confirm that it worked, deal with damaged seed, clean up and record everything.

Follow-up checks

  • Re-inspect treated lots after the time on the label or in your plan. Sieve samples and check traps.
  • Check temperature and moisture again. Hot spots should cool if insects are controlled.
  • If live pests remain, find out why: wrong product, poor coverage, resistance or reinfestation from another area.

Quality of affected seed

Badly damaged lots may need re-cleaning to remove damaged seed and insect dust. Send samples to the laboratory for germination testing. A lot that falls below standard must be downgraded, relabelled or rejected according to company procedure. Never sell seed you know is below the standard on the label.

Clean-up

  1. Clean equipment and store chemicals in the locked chemical store.
  2. Triple rinse empty containers and keep them for approved disposal.
  3. Collect dead rodents with gloves and dispose of them safely.
  4. Remove contaminated sweepings and damaged bags.

Records

RecordPurpose
Lot numbers and locations affectedTraceability
Pest or disease identifiedChoosing future control
Product, rate, date, operatorLegal compliance and safety
Follow-up resultsProof that control worked
Quality test resultsDecision on sale or downgrade

Preventing the next outbreak

Review the causes with your manager. Common causes are poor hygiene, storing seed that was too wet, old lots kept too long, and broken doors or roofs. Adjust the cleaning schedule and monitoring plan.

Key points

  • Find problems early with regular inspection, traps and temperature checks.
  • Identify the pest and how far it has spread before acting.
  • Use hygiene and good storage first; use only registered products by trained people.
  • Fumigation is for qualified fumigators only.
  • Follow up, test seed quality and record every action.
